cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What does JWE define, and under which RFC?
cards.answer: RFC 7516 — the IETF standard for representing encrypted and integrity-protected content as JSON-based data structures; a symmetric Content Encryption Key encrypts the payload under an authenticated encryption algorithm, delivered to recipients via one of five key management modes.

cards.heading: The two-part design
cards.question: What are the two separately-varying concerns in every JWE?
cards.answer: Bulk encryption of the content under a symmetric CEK (always the same mechanism), and delivery of that CEK to each recipient, which varies across the five key management modes.

cards.heading: Header integrity
cards.question: How does JWE protect its header from tampering, including algorithm downgrade?
cards.answer: The base64url-encoded protected header (plus an optional AAD value in the JSON serialization) is passed to the AEAD as Additional Authenticated Data, so tampering with the header invalidates the authentication tag.

cards.heading: Telling JWE and JWS apart
cards.question: How can you cheaply tell a Compact-serialized JWE apart from a JWS?
cards.answer: By dot count — a JWE compact serialization has five base64url segments joined by four dots; a JWS has three segments and two dots.

cards.heading: Avoiding a decryption oracle
cards.question: What must be true of how a JWE recipient handles a malformed encrypted key, and why?
cards.answer: Format, padding and length errors must be reported identically (e.g. substitute a randomly generated CEK and continue) — otherwise an attacker who flips the key-management algorithm header and observes a distinguishable error can recover the CEK, turning the recipient into a decryption oracle.
